result.question: Will hydrogen and ethylene in Transformer 1's oil at site MAIN still be under the IEEE C57.104 Condition 1 limits over the next two days? Use the samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 to forecast both gases 2 days ahead, which is one step per day. For each gas, give the point forecast and an 80% prediction interval for each day. Compare the forecasts with the Condition 1 limits of 100 ppm for hydrogen and 50 ppm for ethylene. If the upper bound of either gas crosses its limit on either day, tell me which gas and which day, and say whether I should bring the next oil sample forward. If the lower bound is also above the limit, call it a likely exceedance, not just a possible one. Before forecasting, check the two series for gaps and fit only on non-null samples. If either gas has fewer than 4 usable samples, don't run a model for it. Instead, project its last value forward using the average daily change between the first and last samples, and label that result as a linear extrapolation with no confidence interval.
result.answer:
The TSFM server has no way to turn IoT telemetry into a file pointer in this session (`materialize_iot` isn't available and I have no file-writing tool), and the only catalogued model (TTM, context 96) can't be fitted on 4 points anyway. So I computed the forecast directly with the same method I'd have run in the recipe — sktime's drift (linear-trend) forecaster with an 80% interval derived from the residual spread of the first differences. Treat the intervals as approximate.

**Data check (2024‑01‑15 → 2024‑01‑18, daily)**
- Hydrogen: 2845, 2950, 2800, 2900 ppm — 4 non‑null samples, no gaps → model path
- Ethylene: 16684, 16500, 16700, 16600 ppm — 4 non‑null samples, no gaps → model path
- No linear-extrapolation fallback was needed for either gas.

**Forecast (drift, 80% PI)**

| Gas | Day | Point (ppm) | 80% PI (ppm) | Condition 1 limit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hydrogen | 2024‑01‑19 | 2,918 | 2,703 – 3,134 | 100 | Likely exceedance |
| Hydrogen | 2024‑01‑20 | 2,937 | 2,595 – 3,278 | 100 | Likely exceedance |
| Ethylene | 2024‑01‑19 | 16,572 | 16,273 – 16,871 | 50 | Likely exceedance |
| Ethylene | 2024‑01‑20 | 16,544 | 16,072 – 17,016 | 50 | Likely exceedance |

**Answer:** No — neither gas will be under its Condition 1 limit on either day. Both hydrogen and ethylene cross their limits on both 2024‑01‑19 and 2024‑01‑20, and because the *lower* bounds are also far above the limits (~26× for H₂, ~320× for C₂H₄), these are likely exceedances, not merely possible ones. In fact, the measured values are already well beyond Condition 4 thresholds (H₂ >1,800 ppm, C₂H₄ >200 ppm), and the ethylene-dominant profile is consistent with a high-energy thermal fault.

**Recommendation:** Yes, bring the next oil sample forward — immediately, not just earlier in the cycle — and run a full DGA (Duval/Rogers) plus inspection. I can trigger `interpret_dga` on the latest sample or raise a work order if you want.
